content.p: The Head Hunters began as a rag-tag bunch of teenage misfits in the Auckland suburb of Glen Innes in the 1960s and grew into one of the largest and best-known gangs in New Zealand. By late 2023 the New Zealand Herald counted several hundred patched members and ranked the club third in size among the country's gangs. Detectives spent years building cases against its senior members for methamphetamine manufacture, extortion and violence, and a decade-long civil action ended in August 2024 with a High Court judge declaring the club an organised criminal group.

The club is also a social group, and a judge accepted that. Its senior member Wayne Doyle says some members have never been convicted and run legitimate businesses, while police allege that crime was organised through the club and a share of its profits passed upward. This account follows the club's growth, the main police operations against it, the court rulings that resulted, and the violence that has marked its recent years.
content.h2: From street gang to national club
content.p: The Herald dates the club's start to about 1967 in Glen Innes, in east Auckland, where it began as a mixed street gang. By 1984 it had moved across the city and opened its first clubrooms in Henderson, in west Auckland. In the early 2000s it divided into three parts: West, which kept the Henderson premises; East, based at Marua Road in Ellerslie; and North, based at Wellsford.

Over the next two decades the Herald said membership rose from several dozen to several hundred. Members now live in Northland, the Bay of Plenty, Wellington and the far south of the South Island, though the club did not formally open chapters in those places. Members there are aligned with the original Auckland chapters. When the Head Hunters "patched over" another gang in Christchurch in 2016 and took its clubrooms, the new South chapter was technically an offshoot of West.

The membership has changed with time. The Herald reported that many newer members are young Pasifika men, while the original members, who grew up together in Glen Innes, tended to be Pākehā or Māori. The club's regular meetings were called "church" until about 2014. Members then voted to rename them "parole board", and later "hui".

In December 2023 the club unveiled a fourth Auckland chapter on the North Shore, the first new Auckland chapter in more than 20 years. It grew out of a crew inside the East chapter known as "Northside". The Herald linked that crew to a feud with the Mongols, a rival gang founded by Australian deportees. The trouble began after a motorcycle repair shop changed hands in 2021, and the Herald described it as a tit-for-tat war of drive-by shootings and arsons that ended with a shooting inside the lobby of a downtown Auckland hotel.

The East chapter's headquarters at 232 Marua Road was the club's best-known base. The Herald described a complex with a gym and swimming pool, where members trained, held "fight nights", stored their motorcycles and gathered for national meetings. Some senior members, including William "Bird" Hines, lived there, the buildings were watched by security cameras, and members were rostered on guard duty. A line from The Godfather was written on a wall.

Wayne Doyle, known inside the club as "the Chief", was a founding member of the East chapter. He had served a sentence for murder and was released in 2001. The Herald reported that he stayed out of trouble with the law after his release and that there was no evidence connecting him to crimes committed by Head Hunters. Police were suspicious about how a man living on benefits had come to control millions of dollars of property.

Police had learned from an earlier failure. In 1999, Operation Mexico targeted Peter "Pedro" Cleven, a Head Hunter accused of making a fortune from cannabis and methamphetamine. His assets were frozen. He was acquitted in 2002 after two controversial trials, the first jury failing to reach a verdict, and under the law then in force the property had to be returned. The Herald reported that police then argued for a change. The Criminal Proceeds Recovery Act 2009 allowed police to seek forfeiture in a civil case, on the balance of probabilities, without a conviction. Introducing the bill in 2007, the then Justice Minister, Mark Burton, said it would allow police to target gang leaders "who do not get their own hands dirty" but enjoy the benefits of other members' crimes.

Between 2014 and 2016 a series of covert investigations led to the seizure of millions of dollars from senior Head Hunters while they served long sentences for drug dealing. In July 2015 police began Operation Coin, aimed at Doyle. A team of about a dozen was expected to finish within three years. It took nearly a decade.

The detectives worked through company and trust records. They found that a company called East 88 Property Holdings had bought 232 Marua Road in the early 2000s for $330,000 when its market value was $500,000, and that most of its shares ended up with a trust of Doyle's. The buildings were leased to a charitable trust, That Was Then This Is Now, which Doyle set up shortly after his release, ostensibly to help former prisoners return to the community. Police analysts believed its charitable purpose was a sham. They counted $17.8 million flowing into six Doyle-linked entities between January 2001 and September 2017, $9.2 million of it in cash, with deposits labelled "rent", "koha", "fight night" or "lottery sales" and $6,638,676 not explained at all.

Police also went back through 20 years of investigation files. One, Operation Ark, involved a syndicate that sold party pills stamped "88", a number the club regards as its own. The syndicate, the Herald reported, had no idea of that and was made to pay the club $1 a pill, later $10,000 a week, nearly $466,000 in all. Police alleged that members paid up to 20 per cent of their criminal earnings to the club as "koha". Doyle rejected that claim. In the bugged conversations from earlier investigations, Doyle was heard only once, in a 2011 inquiry into the kidnapping of a drug supplier, when he could be heard asking about the "koha" and then took the phone to give orders.

On 25 September 2017, armed police searched 232 Marua Road. No charges were laid, and a police release at the time did not name the man it called a "62-year-old beneficiary". Five properties linked to Doyle were restrained by the High Court. The Ministry of Social Development separately alleged that he had claimed $380,992.80 in welfare payments between 1994 and 2017 without declaring income and assets.

Police filed for forfeiture in May 2020, backed by 33 affidavits. Hearings were delayed, partly by arguments that went to the Court of Appeal, and the civil trial opened in the High Court at Auckland in October 2023, six years after the assets were restrained. It ran for four weeks, the longest under the 2009 Act, according to the Herald.

Doyle denied being president of the club. His lawyer, Ron Mansfield KC, acknowledged he was a senior and longstanding member and argued that he had other legitimate sources of income. Doyle told the court that he did not give "green lights" and did not believe in violence. A police witness, Detective Inspector Kevin McNaughton, said Doyle would never use the word president "but we can all tell a leader from how they behave".

Justice Peter Andrew delivered a 154-page judgment on 27 August 2024 after about ten months' deliberation. He accepted that gangs offer companionship, identity and belonging, and that Doyle gave pastoral care to younger members. But he said the Head Hunters were also an organised criminal group, pointing to "the sheer volume" of members convicted of serious offending in the past 20 years. He rejected Doyle's evidence that he held no leadership role as "implausible" and found that he "sits at the pinnacle of the Head Hunters". He also found the charitable trust was a front for the club and was used to launder money. Doyle was ordered to dispose of five Auckland properties, including the Marua Road pad, and about $275,000 in cash seized there was also forfeited.

The figure for the orders differs by outlet. The Herald put the profit forfeiture order at $14.8 million; Newstalk ZB, reporting the judgment the same day, said it totalled "just over $15m". Mansfield said Doyle would appeal.

The largest earlier case was Operation Sylvester. In July 2015, police raided more than 30 properties in Auckland, Waikato and the Bay of Plenty. At the High Court in Auckland, Justice Downs described Hines, then 64, as the architect of a methamphetamine manufacturing operation to which everyone else reported, and called it the work of an "organised criminal enterprise". Hines had been found guilty at trial of 10 charges, including manufacturing methamphetamine, possession for supply and firearms offences. He received 18 years and six months with a minimum of eight years and four months, the judge taking his poor health into account.

Six others were sentenced the same day. Te Here Maihi Maaka received 16 years and two months, Travis Sadler, described as second-in-charge, 18 years and two months, and Falco Maaka 13 years. Peter Atkinson, the cook, who was not a gang member and was hired as a contractor, received 17 years and two months. Thomas Edwardson and John Vijn were also jailed. Detective Superintendent Greg Williams said some of the men were patched Head Hunters or acting for the club and that the group ran a commercial operation. The Herald later reported that Hines died in November 2023, after being released from prison earlier that year on compassionate grounds, while serving a 17-year sentence.

Court cases have also linked patched members to killings. The Herald cited an incident from 2016 in which a man engaged a group of members and associates, called the "Ghost Unit", to abduct a woman caught up in the drug trade; she died after falling from a car boot. Doyle said he had no idea the unit existed at the time.

In November 2023, Samuel Curle, 36, was beaten at an address after arriving there in a Head Hunters hoodie and, the judge said, using standover tactics to try to get drugs. He died in hospital 20 days later. Five people were initially charged with murder. The judge discharged three of them at the end of the Crown case, and Benjamin Gabriel and William Makoare, both patched members, were acquitted of murder and convicted of manslaughter. Justice Graham Lang said they saw his use of the hoodie as an insult to the gang. In December 2025 he sentenced Gabriel to six years and three months and Makoare to six years and six months.

A third case concerned Jayden Mamfredos-Nair, 19, who disappeared in West Auckland in April 2023. His body was found nine months later on a property at Dairy Flat. At the High Court in Auckland, Zak Kameta, a patched member, was sentenced to life with a minimum of 18 years. Matthew Snaylam, a prospect, and an associate, Hassan Al Fadhli, were each given life with a minimum of 17 years. His mother said no sentence could fill the void of his loss.

A new Gangs Act gave police further tools. On 7 March, after a gun was pulled at an address in Torbay on Auckland's North Shore, police issued what RNZ called the first dispersal notice under the Act. It covered occupants of two cars, including three patched Head Hunters, and barred them from associating with each other for seven days. Assistant Commissioner Paul Basham said 403 charges had been laid for insignia breaches and more than 4,000 against gang members over the same period.
